sentences.nl: Hallo, mijn naam is Bart de Pau,, online docent Nederlands.
sentences.en: Hello, my name is Bart de Pau, online Dutch teacher.

sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar les 9 en 10, over bijvoeglijke naamwoorden (adjectieven).
sentences.en: Today we practice sentences, with the grammar from #dutchgrammar lessons 9 and 10, about adjectives.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Today practice we sentences, with the grammar of #dutchgrammar lesson 9 and 10, about adjectives.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Vandaag oefenen we zinnen" follows a typical Dutch word order for present tense: Subject (we) - Verb (oefenen) - Object (zinnen).  
• "Met de grammatica van" uses "met" (with), which is a common preposition to indicate accompaniment or association.  
• "Over bijvoeglijke naamwoorden" uses "over" (about) to introduce the topic or subject matter.  

– Vandaag eten we bij mijn oma. (Today we eat at my grandmother's.)  
– Met de hulp van mijn leraar leerde ik snel. (With the help of my teacher, I learned quickly.)  
– We praten over onze vakantieplannen. (We talk about our vacation plans.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Morgen bespreken we de regels van #dutchgrammar les 11, over werkwoorden. (Tomorrow we discuss the rules of #dutchgrammar lesson 11, about verbs.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
– The use of hashtags like #dutchgrammar reflects the integration of social media and online resources in modern language learning, which is widespread in the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: In deze les gaan Martin en Marieke naar de markt.
sentences.en: In this lesson, Martin and Marieke go to the market.

sentences.nl: Marieke loopt naar de markt vanaf het station.
sentences.en: Marieke walks to the market from the station.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke walks to the market from the station.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The verb "loopt" (walks) is in the present tense. Dutch often uses the simple present to describe current actions.  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to," used to indicate direction.  
• "Vanaf" is a preposition meaning "from," used to indicate the starting point of an action.

Examples:  
• Ik loop naar school. (I walk to school.)  
• Hij fietst vanaf huis. (He bikes from home.)  
• We rijden naar het park. (We drive to the park.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa rijdt naar de stad vanaf haar werk. (Lisa drives to the city from her work.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Markets are popular in the Netherlands, often visited for fresh produce and local products. Many towns have weekly markets that are social and commercial hubs.

sentences.nl: Daar ziet ze Martin.
sentences.en: There she sees Martin.

sentences.nl: Dag Martin!
sentences.en: Hello Martin!

sentences.nl: Dag Marieke!
sentences.en: Hello Marieke!

sentences.nl: Wat een mooie jas!
sentences.en: What a beautiful coat!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• What a beautiful coat!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The phrase "Wat een" is an exclamatory expression used to emphasize admiration or surprise, similar to "What a" in English.  
• "Mooie" is the inflected form of "mooi" (beautiful) used before a noun. In Dutch, adjectives get an '-e' ending when they precede a 'de'-word or plural nouns.  
• "Jas" means "coat."

Examples:  
– Wat een prachtige dag! (What a beautiful day!)  
– Wat een leuk huis! (What a nice house!)  
– Wat een interessante film! (What an interesting film!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wat een geweldige prestatie! (What a great achievement!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch-speaking cultures, complimenting someone's clothing, like "Wat een mooie jas!" is a common way to initiate a positive interaction.

sentences.nl: Is dat een nieuwe jas? — Ja. Dit is een nieuwe jas.
sentences.en: Is that a new coat? — Yes. This is a new coat.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Is dat een nieuwe jas? — Ja. Dit is een nieuwe jas.  
• Is that a new coat? — Yes. This is a new coat.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the basic structure of a yes/no question in Dutch, starting with the verb "is."  
• "Dat" and "dit" are demonstrative pronouns, meaning "that" and "this," respectively.  
• "Een" is the indefinite article "a" or "an."  
• "Nieuwe" is the adjective "new," and it comes before the noun "jas" (coat).

• Additional examples:  
  - Is dat een nieuwe auto? (Is that a new car?)  
  - Dit is een oude fiets. (This is an old bike.)  
  - Heb je een nieuwe bril? (Do you have new glasses?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Is dat een mooie hond? — Ja. Dit is een mooie hond. (Is that a beautiful dog? — Yes. This is a beautiful dog.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, discussing the weather and clothing is common due to the variable climate. Commenting on someone's new coat might be a typical conversation starter.

sentences.nl: Hij is lekker warm.
sentences.en: He is nice and warm.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He is nice warm.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hij" means "he," referring to a male noun or person.  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of "zijn" (to be), used for present tense.  
• "Lekker" often means "tasty," but here it implies comfort or pleasantness, as in "nice and warm."  
• "Warm" is an adjective meaning "warm."  
• Example sentence: "De soep is lekker heet." (The soup is nice and hot.)  
• Example sentence: "Het bed is lekker zacht." (The bed is nice and soft.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De trui is lekker zacht. (The sweater is nice and soft.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, "lekker" is a versatile word that can describe anything pleasant, from food to comfort, and even weather. It highlights the Dutch appreciation for coziness and comfort.

sentences.nl: Buiten is het koud.
sentences.en: It is cold outside.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Outside is it cold.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Buiten" is an adverb meaning "outside" and typically comes at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis.  
• "Is" is the third-person singular present tense of "zijn" (to be).  
• "Het" is a pronoun meaning "it," used here as a dummy subject.  
• "Koud" is an adjective meaning "cold."

• Similar structure:  
  – Binnen is het warm. (Inside it is warm.)  
  – In de tuin is het stil. (In the garden it is quiet.)  
  – Hier is het druk. (Here it is busy.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• In de winter is het donker vroeg. (In the winter, it gets dark early.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, talking about the weather is a common conversation starter. The weather can be quite variable, so it's a frequent topic of discussion.

sentences.nl: Dus een warme jas is belangrijk.
sentences.en: So a warm coat is important.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So a warm coat is important.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dus" is a conjunction meaning "so" or "therefore," often used to indicate a conclusion or result.  
• "Een warme jas" is a noun phrase meaning "a warm coat," where "warme" is the adjective "warm" in its inflected form to agree with the noun "jas."  
• "Is belangrijk" means "is important," using the verb "is" (to be) and the adjective "belangrijk" (important).

• Example Sentences:  
  - "Dus ik ga naar huis." (So I am going home.)  
  - "Een goede nachtrust is belangrijk." (A good night's sleep is important.)  
  - "Het weer is vandaag warm." (The weather is warm today.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dus een stevige paraplu is handig." (So a sturdy umbrella is handy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, having a warm coat is essential due to the often cold and rainy weather, particularly in the fall and winter months. Many Dutch people invest in quality outerwear to stay comfortable year-round.

sentences.nl: Ik wil ook een warme jas.
sentences.en: I also want a warm coat.

sentences.nl: Dit is een oude jas.
sentences.en: This is an old coat.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• This is an old coat.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dit" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "this," used for singular neuter nouns.  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of the verb "zijn" (to be).  
• "Een" is the indefinite article "a" or "an."  
• "Oude" is the adjective "old," and it takes an -e ending because "jas" is a common gender noun with an indefinite article.  
• "Jas" means "coat."

Extra phrases:  
• Dit is een nieuw boek. (This is a new book.)  
• Dat is een mooie foto. (That is a beautiful photo.)  
• Hier is een rode auto. (Here is a red car.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat is een grote hond. (That is a big dog.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, coats are essential due to the often wet and windy climate. Owning a good, durable coat is considered practical.

sentences.nl: Mijn jas is lelijk en een beetje vuil.
sentences.en: My coat is ugly and a bit dirty.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Mijn jas is lelijk en een beetje vuil.  
  • My coat is ugly and a little dirty.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Mijn jas" (My coat) uses the possessive pronoun "mijn" (my), which is used before a noun.  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of "zijn" (to be), used to describe states or conditions.  
• "Lelijk" (ugly) and "vuil" (dirty) are adjectives. In Dutch, adjectives follow the noun they describe when used with "is."  
• "Een beetje" means "a little" or "a bit," often used to moderate an adjective or verb.

### Extra sentences:  
• De auto is snel en een beetje lawaaierig. (The car is fast and a little noisy.)  
• Zijn kamer is groot maar een beetje rommelig. (His room is big but a bit messy.)  
• Het weer is koud en een beetje nat. (The weather is cold and a little wet.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Haar huis is modern en een beetje klein. (Her house is modern and a little small.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness is appreciated, and comments like "lelijk" (ugly) or "vuil" (dirty) might be used more straightforwardly than in some other cultures.

sentences.nl: Ja Martin,, die jas is niet mooi, en ook niet zo schoon.
sentences.en: Yes Martin, that coat is not nice, and not very clean either.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Yes Martin, that coat is not beautiful, and also not so clean.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a simple structure with "ja" (yes) to affirm or agree.  
• "Die" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that," referring to a specific noun mentioned earlier or visible.  
• "Niet mooi" translates to "not beautiful," using "niet" for negation before adjectives.  
• "Ook niet zo" translates to "also not so," indicating additional negative qualities.  
• Example 1: "Die auto is niet snel, en ook niet zo zuinig." (That car is not fast, and also not so economical.)  
• Example 2: "Die film was niet spannend, en ook niet zo grappig." (That movie was not exciting, and also not so funny.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ja Lisa, die schoenen zijn niet goedkoop, en ook niet zo comfortabel." (Yes Lisa, those shoes are not cheap, and also not so comfortable.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of "ja" at the beginning of the sentence can convey agreement or acknowledgment, often seen in conversational Dutch when responding to someone's comment or observation.

sentences.nl: Hier op de markt verkopen ze ook jassen.
sentences.en: Here at the market, they also sell jackets.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Here on the market sell they also coats.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses "Hier op de markt" as an introductory phrase indicating location, followed by the verb "verkopen" (sell) and the subject "ze" (they).  
• "Ook" means "also" and is used to add additional information.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Op school leren ze ook Frans." (At school, they also learn French.)  
  - "In de winkel verkopen ze ook groenten." (In the store, they also sell vegetables.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Op de beurs presenteren ze ook nieuwe technologieën." (At the fair, they also present new technologies.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Markets in the Netherlands are popular places for buying fresh produce and other goods. They often have a variety of stalls, including those that sell clothing like coats.

sentences.nl: Hier is het niet duur.
sentences.en: It is not expensive here.

sentences.nl: Op de markt verkopen ze goedkope jassen.
sentences.en: They sell cheap coats at the market.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• On the market sell they cheap coats.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• This sentence follows the Dutch word order for main clauses: [Time/Place] + [Verb] + [Subject] + [Object].  
• "Op de markt" is a prepositional phrase indicating location.  
• "Verkopen" is the present tense plural form of the verb "verkopen" (to sell), indicating an action performed by "ze" (they).  
• "Goedkope" is an adjective meaning "cheap," modifying the plural noun "jassen" (coats).

Examples:  
• "In de winkel kopen we brood." (In the store, we buy bread.)  
• "Op school leren de kinderen veel." (At school, the children learn a lot.)  
• "Bij de bakker halen zij taart." (At the baker's, they get cake.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Op het strand bouwen ze zandkastelen." (On the beach, they build sandcastles.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Markets are a popular and traditional shopping venue in the Netherlands, often held weekly in towns and cities, where you can find a variety of goods, including fresh produce, clothes, and household items.

sentences.nl: Ik heb het koud.
sentences.en: I am cold.

sentences.nl: En ik wil nu een nieuwe jas!
sentences.en: And I want a new coat now!

sentences.nl: Marieke, help me alsjeblieft.
sentences.en: Marieke, please help me.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke, help me please.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "alsjeblieft" is a polite request meaning "please." It's a contraction of "als je het blieft," which literally translates to "if you please."  
• The structure "Help me alsjeblieft" is a direct imperative sentence, where "help" is the verb in imperative form.  
• In Dutch, when addressing someone directly in a request, you often use their name at the beginning for emphasis and politeness.  
• Examples:  
  - "Jan, kom hier alsjeblieft." (Jan, come here please.)  
  - "Kunt u mij helpen, alsjeblieft?" (Can you help me, please?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Sophie, luister naar mij alsjeblieft." (Sophie, listen to me please.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, using "alsjeblieft" is a common way to soften requests or commands, reflecting the polite and direct communication style typical in the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Dat is goed. Ik help je.
sentences.en: That's good. I will help you.

sentences.nl: We gaan een nieuwe jas uitzoeken.
sentences.en: We are going to pick out a new coat.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• We (We) gaan (go) een (a) nieuwe (new) jas (coat) uitzoeken (to choose).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "We gaan" is present tense and often indicates a future action, similar to "we are going to."  
• "Een nieuwe jas" is a noun phrase in which "nieuwe" is an adjective modifying the noun "jas."  
• "Uitzoeken" is a separable verb, where "uit" is a prefix and "zoeken" is the root verb meaning "to search." In this sentence, it means "to select" or "to choose."

Extra phrases:  
• "We gaan een boek lezen." (We are going to read a book.)  
• "Ik moet een cadeau uitzoeken." (I have to choose a gift.)  
• "Hij gaat een nieuwe auto kopen." (He is going to buy a new car.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Morgen ga ik een nieuwe fiets uitzoeken. (Tomorrow I am going to choose a new bike.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, selecting a new coat for the colder months is quite common, as the weather can be quite chilly and wet. A good coat is considered an essential part of the wardrobe.

sentences.nl: Dat is heel lief van je.
sentences.en: That is very sweet of you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That is very kind of you.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dat" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that."  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of "zijn" (to be) in the present tense.  
• "Heel" is used as an adverb here meaning "very."  
• "Lief" is an adjective meaning "kind" or "sweet."  
• "Van je" translates to "of you," indicating the person responsible for the kindness.

• Extra phrases:  
  - "Dat is heel goed van je." (That is very good of you.)  
  - "Dat is heel aardig van haar." (That is very nice of her.)  
  - "Dat is heel slim van hem." (That is very clever of him.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dat is heel slim van je." (That is very clever of you.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This phrase is commonly used in Dutch to express appreciation for someone's kind actions or words, similar to how "That's very kind of you" is used in English. It's a polite way to acknowledge someone's thoughtfulness.

sentences.nl: Daar is een kraam met jassen.
sentences.en: There is a stall with coats.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• There is a stall with jackets.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "Daar" means "there" and is often used to indicate location or existence.  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of the verb "zijn" (to be), used here to describe existence.  
• "Een kraam" translates to "a stall," and is used for market stalls or booths.  
• "Met" is a preposition meaning "with," indicating what is available at the stall.  
• "Jassen" is the plural form of "jas," meaning "jackets."

Extra examples:  
• "Daar staat een tafel met boeken." (There stands a table with books.)  
• "Er is een winkel met schoenen." (There is a store with shoes.)  
• "Hier is een doos met speelgoed." (Here is a box with toys.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Daar is een kraam met fruit." (There is a stall with fruit.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, market stalls are common in cities and towns, often found in market squares where fresh produce, clothing, and other goods are sold.

sentences.nl: Hallo, ik wil een nieuwe jas.
sentences.en: Hello, I want a new coat.

sentences.nl: Dat kan.
sentences.en: That is possible.

sentences.nl: Een korte jas of een lange jas? — Een korte jas, maar wel warm.
sentences.en: A short coat or a long coat? — A short coat, but warm.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A short coat or a long coat? — A short coat, but indeed warm.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the structure of "een [adjective] [noun]" to describe items, in this case, coats.  
• "Maar wel" is a common phrase used to contrast or emphasize a point, similar to "but indeed" or "but still."  
• "Of" is used here as a conjunction meaning "or," presenting a choice.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Wil je koffie of thee?" (Do you want coffee or tea?)  
  - "Het is koud, maar wel zonnig." (It is cold, but still sunny.)  
  - "Een oude auto of een nieuwe auto?" (An old car or a new car?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een grote hond of een kleine kat? — Een kleine kat, maar wel speels." (A big dog or a small cat? — A small cat, but indeed playful.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, the weather is often unpredictable, so choosing a coat that is both stylish and warm is a common practical consideration.

sentences.nl: Ok. Deze jas is kort.
sentences.en: Okay. This coat is short.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ok. Deze jas is kort.  
  (Okay. This coat is short.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Deze" is a demonstrative pronoun used for "de" words in singular form.  
• The sentence follows the subject-verb-object order typical in Dutch declarative sentences.  
• "Kort" is an adjective meaning "short" and is placed after the verb "is."

Extra phrases/sentences:  
• Deze auto is snel. (This car is fast.)  
• Deze hond is groot. (This dog is big.)  
• Deze stoel is comfortabel. (This chair is comfortable.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Deze tafel is zwaar. (This table is heavy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch people often discuss practicality in fashion, like coat length, due to the climate which can be rainy and windy.

sentences.nl: Maar het is wel een dikke jas.
sentences.en: But it is a thick coat.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But it is indeed a thick coat.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Maar" is a coordinating conjunction meaning "but," used to contrast statements.  
• "Wel" is an adverb that adds emphasis, often translated as "indeed" or "really," to strengthen the statement.  
• "Een dikke jas" means "a thick coat," with "dikke" as the adjective "thick" and "jas" as the noun "coat."

• Example 1: "Het is wel interessant." (It is indeed interesting.)  
• Example 2: "Maar het regent wel." (But it is raining indeed.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Maar het is wel een mooie dag." (But it is indeed a beautiful day.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, discussing the weather and clothing is common, as the weather can be quite variable. A "dikke jas" is often necessary due to the chilly and wet conditions.

sentences.nl: Hmmm. Hij is een beetje te groot.
sentences.en: Hmm. He is a bit too big.

sentences.nl: Nou Martin, misschien ben jij te dun!
sentences.en: Well Martin, maybe you are too thin!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Well Martin, maybe are you too thin!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Nou" is a conversational filler often used to start a sentence, similar to "well" in English.  
• "Misschien" means "maybe" and introduces uncertainty or possibility.  
• The sentence structure "ben jij" is an inversion, placing the verb "ben" (are) before the subject "jij" (you) for emphasis or in questions.  
• "Te" means "too" and is used to indicate an excess, like "te dun" (too thin).

  Extra examples:  
  - "Nou, ik ga naar huis." (Well, I am going home.)  
  - "Misschien komt hij morgen." (Maybe he will come tomorrow.)  
  - "Jij bent te laat!" (You are too late!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Nou, misschien moeten we eerder vertrekken. (Well, maybe we should leave earlier.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, commenting on someone's weight can be sensitive, just as in many other cultures. It's often better approached with care or humor among close friends or family.

sentences.nl: Hier is nog een jas.
sentences.en: Here is another coat.

sentences.nl: Is die niet te klein? — Hmmm. Nee hoor, deze is goed.
sentences.en: Isn't that too small? — Hmm. No, this one is fine.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Is die niet te klein? — Hmmm. Nee hoor, deze is goed.  
  (Is that not too small? — Hmmm. No indeed, this one is good.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Is die niet te klein?" uses the structure for asking a yes/no question, with the verb "is" at the beginning.  
• "Te" is used here to mean "too" in the sense of excessiveness.  
• "Nee hoor" is an informal way of saying "No indeed" or "No, certainly not," where "hoor" adds emphasis or reassurance.  
• "Deze" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "this one," referring to something nearby or previously mentioned.

Extra phrases:  
• "Is het niet te laat?" (Is it not too late?)  
• "Nee hoor, ik kan morgen komen." (No indeed, I can come tomorrow.)  
• "Deze is beter dan die." (This one is better than that one.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Is dat niet te duur? — Nee hoor, dit is een goede prijs." (Is that not too expensive? — No indeed, this is a good price.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common to express opinions directly, which is reflected in the straightforwardness of saying "Nee hoor" to reassure someone.

sentences.nl: Hoe duur is deze jas? — 200 euro
sentences.en: How much does this coat cost? — 200 euros

sentences.nl: Dat is niet goedkoop.
sentences.en: That is not cheap.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That is not cheap.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dat" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that."  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of "zijn" (to be).  
• "Niet" is a negation word meaning "not." It is used to negate adjectives, adverbs, and verbs.  
• "Goedkoop" is an adjective meaning "cheap."

• Extra phrases/sentences:  
  - Deze tas is niet duur. (This bag is not expensive.)  
  - Het weer is niet slecht. (The weather is not bad.)  
  - Hij is niet tevreden. (He is not satisfied.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat huis is niet groot. (That house is not big.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Dat is erg duur!
sentences.en: That is very expensive!

sentences.nl: Kom op Martin!
sentences.en: Come on, Martin!

sentences.nl: Zo arm ben je toch niet? — Maar zo rijk ook niet!
sentences.en: You're not that poor, are you? — But not that rich either!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So poor are you surely not? — But so rich also not!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses inversion, a common Dutch structure where the verb precedes the subject in questions or for emphasis.  
• "Toch" is used for emphasis, implying "surely" or "after all."  
• "Zo" is used to intensify adjectives, meaning "so" or "that."  

Examples:  
– Zo groot ben je toch niet! (You're surely not that tall!)  
– Hij is zo snel als de wind. (He is as fast as the wind.)  
– Zoiets heb ik nog nooit gezien. (I've never seen something like that before.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zo moe ben je toch niet? — Maar zo energiek ook niet! (You're surely not that tired? — But neither are you that energetic!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This type of sentence structure, often used in conversations, reflects the Dutch tendency to be direct yet understated, balancing critique with modesty.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik koop de jas!" follows the standard Dutch word order for simple declarative sentences: Subject (Ik) + Verb (koop) + Object (de jas).  
• "Koop" is the first-person singular present tense of "kopen" (to buy).  
• "De jas" uses the definite article "de" for common gender nouns.  

Extra phrases:  
• "Ik lees het boek." (I read the book.)  
• "Hij eet de appel." (He eats the apple.)  
• "Wij nemen de trein." (We take the train.)

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Heb je honger? — Ja, ik heb honger!  
  (Have you hunger? — Yes, I have hunger!)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Heb je" is the informal second-person singular form of "hebben" (to have) used for questions, where the verb comes first.  
• "Honger" means "hunger," and it is used with the verb "hebben" (to have) in Dutch, unlike English which uses "to be" (to be hungry).  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Heb je dorst?" (Are you thirsty?)  
  - "Ik heb zin in koffie." (I feel like having coffee.)  
  - "Hebben jullie een auto?" (Do you have a car?)
